title: THE WELL WAS NEVER JUST ABOUT WATER
paragraphs:
THE WELL WAS NEVER JUST ABOUT WATER
Rebekah came carrying a jar. Rachel came with sheep. Moses came running from his past. A Samaritan woman came carrying a life she probably wished she could rewrite. Again and again, God chose a well for an encounter—and when Jesus finally sat beside one, the pattern suddenly became impossible to ignore.
There is something strange about the wells in Scripture.
Once you notice it, you cannot easily unsee it.
A servant searching for a bride for Isaac stops at a well—and Rebekah appears.
Jacob, displaced and uncertain about his future, arrives at a well—and Rachel appears.
Moses, a fugitive with blood behind him and no idea what his life has become, collapses beside a well—and the next chapter of his life begins there.
Then centuries later, Jesus Christ sits beside Jacob’s well.
And a woman arrives.
Not Rebekah.
Not Rachel.
Not a celebrated matriarch.
Not someone whose life looked clean enough for a religious portrait.
A Samaritan woman with a complicated history.
And suddenly all those earlier wells begin to feel like echoes.
But we need to be careful here.

The Bible never says, “Every well symbolizes the same thing,” and we should not force Scripture into an allegory God did not give us. Wells were essential places in the ancient world. People needed water. Flocks needed water. Communities gathered around water.
Yet the biblical narratives themselves undeniably place several enormous turning points beside wells.
So perhaps the question is not, What magical symbolism did wells possess?
Perhaps the better question is:
Why does Scripture repeatedly show God meeting people in ordinary places of thirst, transition, vulnerability, exile, work, and need?
Because maybe that is where some of us are standing right now.
Not inside a dramatic miracle.
Not on a mountaintop.
Just carrying the same jar again.
Doing the same job.
Living with the same memories.
Trying to survive another ordinary day.
And having absolutely no idea that God may already be standing beside the place where we came merely looking for enough water to get through today.
Rebekah did not wake up knowing Genesis 24 would become Genesis 24.
Think about that.
Abraham had sent his servant to find a wife for Isaac. The servant reached the region of Abraham’s relatives and stopped near a source of water. He prayed for God’s guidance.
Then Scripture says something breathtaking.
Before he had finished speaking, Rebekah appeared with her jar.
The Hebrew preserves the immediacy beautifully:
וְהִנֵּה רִבְקָה — wəhinneh Rivqah.
“And behold—Rebekah.”
She was simply coming for water.
She did not know that somebody had been praying before she arrived.
She did not know that her ordinary act of carrying a water jar was intersecting with Abraham’s family and the unfolding covenant story.
She was living an ordinary moment while God was working through extraordinary providence.
That should humble us.
Because sometimes we demand that God announce His work with thunder.
We want the dream.
The unmistakable sign.
The dramatic opening of heaven.
But Rebekah walked toward her future carrying a jar.
Some of the most important moments of your life may initially look painfully ordinary.
A conversation.
A delay.
An interruption.
A person you almost ignored.
A door you did not expect.
An ordinary act of obedience performed while nobody was applauding.

Rebekah’s character also mattered. The servant’s test concerned hospitality, and her response went beyond merely giving him a drink; she offered water for his camels as well. Later, when her family asked whether she would actually leave with the servant, the Hebrew records her answer with stunning simplicity:
אֵלֵךְ — ’elekh.
“I will go.”
Two words in English.
One enormous surrender.
She could not see the entire road.
She went.
And eventually Isaac took Rebekah as his wife and loved her.
A woman went to draw water and walked into a story larger than herself.
Then there was Rachel.
Jacob arrived in the land of his relatives after leaving home under deeply fractured circumstances. His family story was already messy—favoritism, deception, stolen blessing, anger, separation.
Then he saw a well.
Genesis 29 describes flocks gathered around it and a large stone over its opening.
And while Jacob was still speaking with the shepherds, Rachel came with her father’s sheep.
The Hebrew narration says:
וְרָחֵל בָּאָה — wəRachel ba’ah.
“Rachel came.”
She was working.
She was shepherding.
Another ordinary day.
Another well.
Another life-changing encounter.
Jacob rolled away the stone and watered Laban’s flock. Soon he kissed Rachel and wept.
But Scripture refuses to turn their story into a sanitized romance.
Jacob loved Rachel, yes.
He also entered years of family dysfunction.
Laban deceived him.
Leah became caught in a painful marriage.
Rachel experienced infertility before eventually bearing Joseph.
Jealousy entered the household.
Competition entered the household.
Heartbreak entered the household.
The Bible does not airbrush its families.
That matters.
Because Scripture is not a museum filled with perfect people.
It is the record of a holy God working through catastrophically imperfect human beings.
And maybe that is why you should stop believing the lie that your family history automatically disqualifies your future.
God is not endorsing the sin in our stories when He redeems people inside those stories.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Grace is God refusing to let evil have the final word.
Then Moses reaches his well.
And his arrival feels completely different.
Rebekah came carrying a jar.
Rachel came with sheep.
Moses came running.
He had killed an Egyptian. Pharaoh learned about it and sought his life. Moses fled Egypt and entered Midian.
Then comes one of the loneliest sentences imaginable:
וַיֵּשֶׁב עַל־הַבְּאֵר — wayyeshev ‘al-habbe’er.
He “sat down by the well.”
The Hebrew noun בְּאֵר — be’er means a well.
Moses—the man who had once lived within Pharaoh’s world—is now a fugitive sitting beside one.
No palace.
No position.
No clear future.
Just a man who had tried to intervene against injustice in a sinful way and now had to live with the consequences.
Somebody reading this understands that kind of place.
You thought your life would look different by now.
You made decisions you cannot reverse.
You reacted in anger.
You trusted someone you should not have trusted.
You became someone you barely recognize.
Maybe nobody knows the entire story.
Maybe your social media profile looks fine.
Maybe you still attend church.
Maybe you still say, “God is good,” because you know the correct vocabulary.
But somewhere inside you is a Moses sitting beside a well whispering:
What have I done?
And here is where cheap grace would tell you that your sin does not matter.
Biblical grace tells you something infinitely better.
Your sin matters enough that Christ had to die.
And Christ’s blood is sufficient enough that repentant sinners do not have to remain defined by what they have done.
Moses’ failure was real.
So was God's future work in him.
The well was not Moses’ destination.
Midian would become a long wilderness classroom. Moses would become a shepherd before God sent him back to confront Pharaoh and shepherd Israel.
The fugitive sitting beside the well did not yet understand the man God would shape him into.
Please hear this carefully:
Your worst chapter does not become holy merely because God redeems you from it. But your worst chapter does not possess greater authorship than God either.
Repentance does not rewrite history by pretending the sin never happened.
Grace rewrites the sinner.
That is different.
That is Christianity.
And then...
Jesus comes to a well.
Now the pattern reaches its climax.
John 4 tells us that Jacob’s well was there and that Jesus, tired from His journey, sat beside it.
Jesus was genuinely weary.
The eternal Son had truly taken human nature.
And there beside an ancient well, the incarnate Christ waited.
Then she came.
A Samaritan woman.
John tells us it was about the sixth hour. Jesus said:
“Give Me a drink.”
She was surprised.
A Jewish man was speaking to a Samaritan woman.
But Jesus had not come merely to discuss water.
He told her that if she knew the gift of God and knew who was speaking to her, she would ask Him—and He would give her living water.
She initially thought in physical categories.
The well was deep.
Jesus had no drawing vessel.
Where would this water come from?
Then Christ said something that reaches beyond Sychar and straight into every thirsty human heart.
In Greek, John 4:14 describes what Christ gives becoming within the recipient:
πηγὴ ὕδατος ἁλλομένου εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον
“a spring of water welling up into eternal life.”
Notice the word John uses:
πηγή — pēgē.
A spring.
A fountain.
The woman came looking for water outside herself.
Jesus began speaking about life God would put within.
That is the Gospel.
Religion without Christ keeps sending thirsty people back to the same bucket.
Try harder.
Hide better.
Perform more convincingly.
Make everyone believe you are okay.
Manage the image.
Protect the reputation.
Carry the jar.
Lower it again.
Pull it back up.
Drink.
Become thirsty.
Repeat.
Jesus offers something the world cannot manufacture.
Life.
Not self-improvement disguised as Christianity.
Not merely religious information.
Not emotional excitement that disappears Monday morning.
Christ Himself.
And then Jesus touches the place she probably would have preferred to keep hidden.
Her relationships.
Jesus tells her to call her husband.
She answers that she has no husband.
Christ reveals that He knows her history: she has had five husbands, and the man she currently has is not her husband.
Do not miss what happens.
Jesus exposes her without exploiting her.
He tells the truth without abandoning her.
He does not flatter her sin.
He does not redefine holiness to protect her feelings.
But neither does He treat her as disposable.
This is what so many people misunderstand about Jesus.
Christ is more holy than the religious hypocrite thinks...
and more merciful than the ashamed sinner dares hope.
He knows.
Everything.
The relationship.
The browser history.
The bitterness.
The secret messages.
The addiction.
The jealousy.
The money.
The pride.
The resentment.
The thing you did.
The thing done to you.
The version of yourself you carefully present to church people.
The version your family sees.
The version nobody sees.
He knows.
And still He speaks.
That is terrifying until you understand the Gospel.
Because the One who knows everything is the One who went to the cross.

The conversation eventually turns to worship. The woman raises the dispute over the proper place of worship, and Jesus refuses to leave the issue at geography. He speaks of the Father seeking those who worship in spirit and truth.
Then the woman speaks of the coming Messiah.
And Jesus reveals Himself to her.
The person she needed was already sitting beside the place where she had been trying to satisfy her thirst.
Maybe that is the thread connecting these wells.
Not that every well carries some secret mystical code.
But that throughout Scripture, wells become remarkably fitting locations for turning points because wells are places of need.
You do not approach a well because you have no thirst.
You approach because something living requires water.
Rebekah approached with a jar.
Rachel approached with sheep.
Moses approached with nowhere else to go.
The Samaritan woman approached because ordinary human life required another trip for water.
And Jesus used that physical thirst to reveal a deeper thirst.
We do the same thing she did.
Different wells.
Same thirst.
We lower the bucket into romance.
Maybe somebody will finally make me feel wanted.
We lower it into money.
Maybe enough security will silence my fear.
Into pornography.
Maybe pleasure will numb the emptiness.
Into attention.
Maybe enough likes will convince me I matter.
Into success.
Maybe achievement will make the shame disappear.
Into religion.
Maybe if I look spiritual enough, nobody—including God—will notice what is happening underneath.
Into another relationship.
Another purchase.
Another promotion.
Another drink.
Another secret.
Another distraction.
Another Sunday where we sing about living water while quietly drinking from wells that cannot satisfy us.
Bucket down.
Bucket up.
Drink.
Thirst.
Bucket down.
Bucket up.
Drink.
Thirst.
And Jesus is still saying:
You are thirsty for something creation was never designed to become for you.
Your spouse cannot be your Savior.
Your children cannot be your Savior.
Your pastor cannot be your Savior.
Your career cannot be your Savior.
Your church attendance cannot be your Savior.
Your morality cannot be your Savior.
Your pain cannot excuse your sin.
Your past cannot cleanse your conscience.
And you cannot save yourself.
Only Jesus Christ saves sinners.
The deepest meaning of John 4 is not, “Believe in yourself because you are secretly wonderful.”
It is almost the opposite.
You are desperately thirsty...
and the Water has come to you.
Jesus did not merely come to improve the Samaritan woman's self-esteem.
He came revealing Himself as Messiah.
And the same Gospel reaches us through His death and resurrection.
Christ lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He rose bodily from the grave.
Forgiveness is offered through Him.
Reconciliation with God is found in Him.
Eternal life is found in Him.
And the response is not merely admiration.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Stop protecting the very chains from which you are begging God to free you.
Stop calling darkness “complicated” when Christ is calling you into light.
Stop assuming that because Jesus knows your scandal, He must be finished with you.
The cross proves something astonishing:
Jesus already knew the full cost of redeeming sinners when He chose the road to Calvary.
That is why our message will always be:
Not scandal to excuses.
Not scandal to self-acceptance without repentance.
Not scandal to pretending consequences disappear.
Scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites the adulterer into the forgiven.
The proud into the humbled.
The enslaved into the liberated.
The enemy into the adopted child.
The religious performer into the worshiper.
The ashamed into the witness.
And something beautiful happens in John 4.
The woman who came carrying a water jar eventually leaves it behind and goes into the town.
The woman who entered the scene needing water becomes a person telling others about Jesus.
“Come, see...”
That movement is astonishing.
She encountered Christ.
Then she told people.
And they came toward Him.
That is evangelism stripped of performance.
Come see the One I encountered.
Maybe that is why this article found you.
Not so you could simply say, “Interesting Bible connection.”
Maybe there is a jar you need to put down.
Maybe there is a well you need to stop revisiting.
Maybe there is sin you need to confess.
Maybe you have been surviving on church culture without actually surrendering to Christ.
Maybe you love Christian content but have resisted the Christ the content is supposed to proclaim.
Maybe you have spent years managing your scandal when Jesus has been calling you into grace.
Then stop hiding.
Right here.
Right now.
You do not need impressive religious language.
Come honestly.

“Jesus Christ, I have sinned. I cannot save myself. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Turn my heart from sin. I surrender myself to You. Be Lord of my life. Teach me to follow You.”
Words themselves are not magic.
Christ saves.
So come to Him genuinely.
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded believer sees and realizes, I am not the only one fighting.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God. It does not. We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
But if this Gospel truth helped you, sharing it can place that truth in front of someone you may never realize is thirsty.
Send it to the family member you keep praying for.
Share it with the person who believes their past has permanently disqualified them.
Even send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is only about polished religious people pretending they have never been broken.
Let them meet Jesus at the well.
There may come a night when the old thirst returns and you need to remember that returning to the old well will never become living water simply because you are lonely.
Our purpose is to keep putting Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ in front of people who desperately need Him.
If this ministry is helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, fight sin, heal, repent, endure, and keep walking when you wanted to quit, consider standing with the mission.
Not as a transaction with God.
As a mission.
A Rachel carrying responsibilities while her future is approaching.
A Moses sitting beside the ruins of his own decisions wondering whether God could possibly use him again.
Or a Samaritan woman carrying the same jar back to the same well, desperately hoping something outside her can finally satisfy what is broken inside.
And perhaps your share becomes the small doorway through which they hear:
There is living water.
There is forgiveness.
There is a cross.
There is an empty tomb.
There is repentance.
There is grace.
There is still a Savior.
His name is Jesus.
And maybe the most haunting truth about all these wells is this:
You thought you came because you were thirsty. You never imagined Christ was already waiting at the place where your thirst would finally tell the truth about you.
